questions.question: What is the approximate time period of second phase of the green revolution in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**mid- 1970s to mid-1980s**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Green Revolution** in India was a period when Indian agriculture was converted into an industrial system due to the adoption of modern methods and technology. It is generally categorized into **two distinct phases**.
 
• The **second phase** of the Green Revolution approximately spanned from the **mid-1970s to the mid-1980s**. ***Hence, the correct answer is mid- 1970s to mid-1980s.***
 
• During this **second phase**, the **High-Yielding Variety (HYV) technology** spread to a much larger number of states and benefited a more diverse range of crops beyond just wheat and rice.
 
• While the **first phase** (mid-1960s to mid-1970s) was restricted to affluent states like **Punjab**, **Haryana**, and **Western Uttar Pradesh**, the **second phase** saw expansion into states like **Andhra Pradesh**, **Tamil Nadu**, and parts of the **Eastern region**.
 
• This geographical spread was crucial in ensuring that the benefits of increased **food grain production** were distributed more equitably across the country, helping India move closer to total **food self-sufficiency**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Origins of Green Revolution:**

 
 
• The revolution was initiated in the **1960s** by introducing **Mexican wheat varieties**.
 
• **M.S. Swaminathan** is known as the **Father of the Green Revolution in India** for his leadership and role in introducing and further developing **HYV** wheat varieties.
 
• Globally, **Norman Borlaug** is hailed as the **Father of the Green Revolution** and was awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize** in **1970** for his work.
 
 
 
• **Core Components:**
 
 
• **HYV Seeds:** These seeds had a higher yield potential compared to traditional seeds but required a reliable supply of **water** and the correct proportion of **fertilizers** and **pesticides**.
 
• **Irrigation:** The success of the revolution was heavily dependent on **assured irrigation facilities**, leading to the construction of various **dams** and **tube wells**.
 
• **Chemical Inputs:** Increased use of **chemical fertilizers**, **pesticides**, and **weedicides** was necessary to protect and nourish the high-yielding crops.
 
 
 
• **Economic Impact:**
 
 
• It resulted in a significant increase in the **productivity** of food grains, especially **wheat** and **rice**.
 
• The surplus production allowed the government to maintain a **buffer stock** through the **Food Corporation of India (FCI)**, which could be used during times of food shortage.
 
• It enabled the **commercialization of agriculture** as farmers began producing for the market rather than just for **subsistence**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Phases Comparison:**

 
 
• **Phase I (mid-1960s to mid-1970s):** Characterized by the use of **HYV seeds** primarily in wheat-growing regions like **Punjab** and **Haryana**.
 
• **Phase II (mid-1970s to mid-1980s):** Marked by the spread of technology to other states and inclusion of **rice** and other crops in the **HYV** net.
 
 
 
• **Government Policy:**
 
 
• The government provided **loans at low-interest rates** and **subsidized fertilizers** so that small farmers could also afford the necessary inputs.
 
• This intervention was vital to prevent the "rich getting richer" syndrome and to make the **Green Revolution** inclusive for small-scale landholders.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Concerns:** While the revolution solved **hunger**, it later faced criticism for **soil degradation**, **depletion of groundwater**, and the loss of **biodiversity** due to **monocropping**.

questions.question: In India, as per the Industrial Policy Resolution 1956, the second category consisted of industries in which the ______.

options.text: private sector could supplement the efforts of public sector
only foreign private sector would be entertained
public sector units had no role
private sector had sole authority to start new units

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**private sector could supplement the efforts of public sector**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) of 1956** was adopted by the Indian Parliament in **April 1956**. It formed the basis of the **Second Five Year Plan (1956-1961)**, which focused heavily on the development of heavy industries.
 
• This resolution classified industries into three distinct categories based on the role the state and private players would play. The **second category**, often referred to as **Schedule B**, consisted of industries that were to be progressively state-owned.
 
• In this second category, the **State** would take the initiative of setting up new industrial units, but the **private sector** was given the opportunity to **supplement the efforts of the State**. ***Hence, the correct answer is the private sector could supplement the efforts of the public sector.***
 
• There were **12 industries** listed under this second category. These included industries like **aluminum**, **other non-ferrous metals**, **machine tools**, **ferro-alloys**, **basic and intermediate products required by chemical industries**, **antibiotics**, **fertilizers**, and **synthetic rubber**.
 
• The primary objective of this categorization was to ensure that the government maintained control over the "commanding heights" of the economy while allowing private enterprise to contribute to national growth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Schedule A (First Category):**

 
 
• This category comprised **17 industries** which were the **exclusive responsibility of the State**. No new units could be started by the private sector in these fields.
 
• Examples included **arms and ammunition**, **atomic energy**, **iron and steel**, **heavy plant and machinery**, **coal and lignite**, **mineral oils**, **mining of iron ore**, and **railway transport**.
 
 
 
• **Schedule C (Third Category):**
 
 
• This category included all the **remaining industries** not mentioned in Schedules A or B.
 
• These were generally **left to the private sector**, but they were still subject to the framework of social and economic policy of the State, primarily through **industrial licensing**.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Licensing (The License Raj):**
 
 
• Even for industries in the private sector, the 1956 policy mandated a **license** from the government to start a new industry or expand existing capacity.
 
• This system was used to promote **regional equality**; it was easier to obtain a license if the industrial unit was proposed in an **economically backward area**.
 
• Tax benefits and lower electricity tariffs were also provided to industries established in backward regions to encourage **balanced regional development**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **IPR 1956** is often called the **Economic Constitution of India** or the "Bible of State Capitalism" because it defined the **socialist pattern of society** as the ultimate goal of India's economic policy.
 
• It was heavily influenced by the **Mahalanobis Model**, which emphasized the development of capital goods industries to achieve long-term self-reliance.
 
• The resolution replaced the **Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948**, reflecting the shift toward a more dominant role for the **public sector** in the Indian economy.
 
• The policy remained the guiding principle for Indian industrialization until the **New Economic Policy of 1991**, which introduced **liberalization, privatization, and globalization (LPG)**.

questions.question: Ionosphere is a part of _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Thermosphere**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Ionosphere** is a significant layer of the Earth's atmosphere that is primarily considered a part of the **Thermosphere**. It extends from an altitude of about **80 kilometers (50 miles)** to **400 kilometers (250 miles)** above the Earth's surface.
 
• This layer is characterized by the presence of **ions** and **free electrons**, which are created through the process of **photoionization**. This happens when high-energy **Solar Radiation** (such as **UV rays** and **X-rays**) hits the atoms and molecules in the upper atmosphere, knocking off electrons.
 
• The most critical function of the **Ionosphere** is its ability to reflect **radio waves**. Long-distance **radio communication** is possible because these waves are reflected back to Earth by the charged particles in this layer, rather than escaping into space.
 
• Within the **Thermosphere**, temperatures increase rapidly with altitude due to the absorption of intense **solar energy**. Despite the high temperatures (which can reach **1,500°C** or more), the air is so thin that it would not feel "hot" to a human.
 
• The **Ionosphere** is also the region where spectacular natural light displays known as **Auroras** (Aurora Borealis and Aurora Australis) occur, caused by the interaction between the **solar wind** and the Earth's **magnetic field**.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Thermosphere.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Troposphere:**

 
 
• This is the **lowest layer** of the atmosphere, extending from the Earth's surface up to an average height of **13 kilometers** (about **8 km** at the **poles** and **18 km** at the **equator**).
 
• It contains approximately **75% to 80%** of the atmosphere's total mass and nearly all of its **water vapor** and **dust particles**.
 
• All **weather phenomena**, such as **cloud formation**, **rainfall**, and **storms**, occur in this layer. The temperature **decreases** with increasing height at a rate of **6.5°C per kilometer**.
 
 
 
• **Stratosphere:**
 
 
• Located above the Troposphere, it extends up to a height of **50 kilometers**. This layer is very dry and contains very few clouds.
 
• The **Stratosphere** houses the **Ozone Layer** (Ozonosphere), which protects life on Earth by absorbing harmful **Ultraviolet (UV) radiation** from the sun.
 
• Due to the absence of weather disturbances and vertical air currents, this layer is considered **ideal for flying jet aircraft**.
 
 
 
• **Mesosphere:**
 
 
• The **Mesosphere** lies above the Stratosphere and extends up to **80 kilometers**. It is known as the **coldest layer** of the atmosphere, with temperatures dropping as low as **-90°C**.
 
• This is the layer where most **meteors** burn up upon entering the Earth's atmosphere due to **friction** with the air.
 
 
 
• **Exosphere:**
 
 
• This is the **outermost layer** of the atmosphere, beginning at the top of the Thermosphere and extending into **outer space**.
 
• The air in the **Exosphere** is extremely thin, consisting mainly of light gases like **Helium** and **Hydrogen**, which eventually drift out into space.
 
• This layer is where many **satellites** orbit the Earth.

questions.question: In humans, rings of cartilage are present in the ___.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**throat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the human anatomy, the **throat** contains the **trachea** (commonly known as the **windpipe**), which is reinforced by **rings of cartilage**.
 
• These rings are specifically **C-shaped** and are made of **hyaline cartilage**. They are stacked one above the other along the length of the **trachea**. ***Hence, the option "throat" is correct.***
 
• The primary **function** of these **cartilaginous rings** is to provide structural support and prevent the **trachea** from collapsing. This ensures that the airway remains open even when there is negative pressure during **inhalation**.
 
• The **C-shaped** structure is crucial because the open part of the "C" faces the **posterior** side, where the **esophagus** is located. This allows the **esophagus** to expand slightly into the space of the **trachea** when a person swallows a large bolus of **food**.
 
• Without these **rings**, the soft tissue of the **throat** would likely collapse during breathing, leading to **asphyxiation** or respiratory distress.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Cartilage:** It is a flexible, resilient **connective tissue** that is found in various parts of the body. It is composed of specialized cells called **chondrocytes** that produce a large amount of **collagenous extracellular matrix**.
 
• **Types of Cartilage:**
 
 
• **Hyaline Cartilage:** This is the most common type, found in the **trachea**, **nose**, and at the ends of **long bones** (articular cartilage).
 
• **Elastic Cartilage:** Contains more elastic fibers, providing flexibility to structures like the **external ear** (pinna) and the **epiglottis**.
 
• **Fibrocartilage:** The strongest type, found in **intervertebral discs** and the **pubic symphysis**, designed to withstand heavy pressure.
 
 
 
• **Other Options Analysis:**
 
 
• **Stomach:** The **stomach** is a muscular organ that lacks **cartilaginous rings**. Its structure is primarily composed of **smooth muscle** layers and a **mucosal lining**.
 
• **Mouth:** The **mouth** consists of the **tongue**, **teeth**, and **palate**. While the hard palate has a bony base, there are no **rings of cartilage** present here.
 
• **Ear:** While the **outer ear** (pinna) is made of **elastic cartilage**, it does not contain structural **rings** like the respiratory tract.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The human **trachea** typically contains **16 to 20** individual **cartilaginous rings**.
 
• The **trachea** extends from the **larynx** (voice box) down to the **carina**, where it bifurcates into the left and right **primary bronchi**.
 
• The **bronchi** also contain **cartilage**, but as they branch further into **bronchioles**, the **cartilage** disappears and is replaced by **smooth muscle**.
 
• The open ends of the **C-shaped rings** are connected by the **trachealis muscle**, which can contract to narrow the **trachea**, increasing the force of **air** during **coughing**.
 
• The inner lining of the **trachea** is composed of **pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium** with **goblet cells** that produce **mucus** to trap foreign particles.

questions.question: The Guptas issued a large number of gold coins called ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dinaras**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Gupta Empire**, which flourished from the **4th to 6th century CE**, is renowned for issuing the **largest number of gold coins** in ancient Indian history. These gold coins were professionally known as **Dinaras**.
 
• The term **Dinara** is believed to have been derived from the **Roman currency** known as **Denarius**, reflecting the strong trade links between India and the Western world during that era.
 
• The **Gupta gold coins** were not only a medium of exchange but also served as a medium for **royal propaganda**, depicting the kings in various poses such as playing the **Veena**, hunting lions, or performing religious sacrifices.
 
• The early **Gupta coinage** was heavily influenced by the **Kushana** style, but later rulers introduced indigenous elements, including **Sanskrit inscriptions** and figures of Indian deities like **Lakshmi** and **Garuda**.
 
• While the Guptas issued the **maximum number** of gold coins, it is noted by historians that the **purity of gold** in these coins gradually declined during the later part of the dynasty compared to the high-purity coins of the **Kushanas**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Tanka and Jital:**

 
 
• The **Tanka** (silver coin) and **Jital** (copper coin) were the standard currencies introduced much later by the **Delhi Sultanate**.
 
• **Iltutmish**, the Sultan of the **Slave Dynasty**, is credited with introducing these coins in the **13th century** to stabilize the economy of the Sultanate. ***Hence, options 2 and 3 are incorrect in the context of the Guptas.***
 
 
 
• **Rupakas (Silver Coins):**
 
 
• The Guptas also issued silver coins known as **Rupakas**.
 
• The issuance of silver coins was primarily started by **Chandragupta II** (Vikramaditya) after his successful military campaign and victory over the **Saka Kshatrapas** of Western India.
 
 
 
• **Copper Coins:**
 
 
• While gold and silver were prominent, **copper coins** were also issued by Gupta rulers like **Ramagupta** and **Chandragupta II**, though they are found in much smaller quantities compared to the **Dinaras**.
 
 
 
• **Economic Significance:**
 
 
• The abundance of **Dinaras** indicates a flourishing **money economy** and significant **long-distance trade**. However, the scarcity of copper coins in later periods suggests a possible decline in local trade or a shift towards **barter systems** for daily transactions.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Samudragupta:** Known as the **"Napoleon of India,"** his coins are famous for the **"Lyrist type"** depicting him playing the **Veena**, which highlights his interest in music and art.
 
• **Chandragupta I:** He is often credited with the **"King-Queen type"** coins, which featured him alongside his wife **Kumaradevi**, a princess of the **Lichchhavi** clan.
 
• **Iconography:** The reverse side of the **Gupta gold coins** frequently featured the **Goddess Lakshmi** seated on a lotus, symbolizing prosperity, which became a hallmark of Indian numismatics.
 
• **Decline of Coinage:** Following the **Huna invasions** and the internal disintegration of the empire in the **6th century**, the standard and quantity of the **Dinaras** saw a sharp decline, marking the end of the **Golden Age** of Indian coinage.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a reason for Magadh's dominance over other Mahajanapadas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Access to the Arabian Sea**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Magadha** emerged as the most powerful **Mahajanapada** between the **6th and 4th centuries BCE** due to several geographical and strategic advantages.
 
• **Fertile river plains**: Magadha was situated in the **Gangetic valley**, where the confluence of the **Ganges**, **Son**, and **Gandak** rivers provided exceptionally fertile land. This led to a massive **agricultural surplus**, which allowed the state to maintain a large standing army and a complex administrative machinery. ***Hence, statement 1 is a correct reason for its dominance.***
 
• **Natural fortifications**: The first capital of Magadha, **Rajgir** (then known as **Rajgriha**), was surrounded by **five hills**, making it virtually impregnable to enemies. Later, the capital was shifted to **Pataliputra**, which served as a **water fort** (Jaladurga) because it was situated at the junction of major rivers, providing both protection and a means of communication. ***Hence, statement 2 is a correct reason for its dominance.***
 
• **Rich iron deposits**: Magadha had easy access to **iron ore mines** located in the **Chota Nagpur plateau** (modern-day **Jharkhand**). This allowed the Magadhan army to manufacture superior **iron weapons** and improved agricultural tools, giving them an edge over rivals who relied on copper or bronze. ***Hence, statement 3 is a correct reason for its dominance.***
 
• **Access to the Arabian Sea**: Magadha was an inland kingdom located in **Eastern India** (modern-day **Bihar**). While it controlled riverine trade through the **Bay of Bengal**, it had no direct **access to the Arabian Sea**, which is located on the **Western coast** of India. ***Hence, statement 4 is NOT a reason for its dominance and is the correct answer.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The 16 Mahajanapadas**: According to the **Buddhist text Anguttara Nikaya** and the **Jaina text Bhagavati Sutra**, there were **16 great kingdoms** known as **Mahajanapadas** in ancient India during the **Vedic period**.
 
• **Military Innovation**: Magadha was the first kingdom to use **elephants** on a large scale in warfare. These elephants were sourced from the dense **forests of the east** (modern **Odisha** and **Bengal**) and were used to smash enemy forts and formations.
 
• **Ambitious Rulers**: The rise of Magadha is also attributed to the policies of its powerful kings like **Bimbisara**, **Ajatashatru**, and **Mahapadma Nanda**. **Bimbisara** (Haryanka Dynasty) used **matrimonial alliances** and conquests to expand his territory.
 
• **Trade and Commerce**: The control over the **Ganges river** trade route facilitated **economic prosperity**. Taxes collected from trade and agriculture provided the **Mauryan** and pre-Mauryan rulers with the wealth needed to build the first great **Indian Empire**.
 
• **Strategic Capitals**: **Udayin**, the successor of **Ajatashatru**, shifted the capital to **Pataliputra** (modern **Patna**) to better control the trade routes and the vast plains of Northern India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Haryanka Dynasty**: Founded by **Bimbisara** in **544 BCE**, this was the first significant dynasty of Magadha. **Ajatashatru**, his son, famously used new war engines like the **Rathamusala** (scythed chariot) and **Mahashilakantaka** (a catapult-like engine).
 
• **Nanda Dynasty**: Founded by **Mahapadma Nanda**, who is often called the "**first empire builder**" of Indian history. The Nandas maintained a massive army, including **200,000 infantry** and **6,000 war elephants**, which allegedly discouraged **Alexander the Great** from invading further into India in **326 BCE**.
 
• **Mauryan Empire**: Following the Nandas, **Chandragupta Maurya** established the **Mauryan Empire** in **322 BCE** with the help of **Chanakya**, making Magadha the center of the first pan-Indian empire.

questions.question: What name did ancient Chinese texts use for India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Yintu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In ancient **Chinese** literature, the term **Yintu** (also written as **Yin-tu** or **Yindu**) was used to refer to the Indian subcontinent. ***Hence, option 3 is correct.***
 
• The name **Yintu** is a phonetic transliteration of the **Sanskrit** word **Sindhu**, which is the name of the river **Indus**.
 
• The famous **Chinese** Buddhist monk and scholar **Xuanzang** (Hsuan-tsang), who visited **India** during the **7th century AD** (specifically between **629 AD** and **645 AD**), standardized this name in his writings.
 
• Before **Xuanzang**, various other names were found in **Chinese** records, such as **Shendu** (used during the **Han Dynasty**) and **Tiandu**, all of which were early attempts to capture the sound of **Sindhu**.
 
• **Xuanzang** noted that the name **Yintu** was more accurate than previous versions to describe the vast land located to the west of **China**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Bharat**:

 
 
• It is the indigenous and constitutional name of **India**.
 
• The name is derived from the ancient **Bharata** tribe or the legendary **King Bharata**, a descendant of the **Puru** dynasty.
 
• It is mentioned in ancient **Sanskrit** texts like the **Rigveda** and the **Puranas**, where **Bharatavarsha** refers to the geographical entity of the subcontinent.
 
 
 
• **Indica**:
 
 
• This is the title of a historical account written by **Megasthenes**, a **Greek** ethnographer and ambassador.
 
• He was sent to the court of **Chandragupta Maurya** around **300 BC** by the **Hellenistic** king **Seleucus I Nicator**.
 
• The book provides vital information about the **Mauryan** administration, social classes, and the city of **Pataliputra**.
 
 
 
• **Sindhu**:
 
 
• This is the **Sanskrit** name for the **Indus River**, one of the longest rivers in **Asia**.
 
• The **Persians**, who had difficulty pronouncing 'S', called the river **Hindu** and the land **Hindustan**.
 
• The **Greeks** later dropped the 'H' to call the river **Indos**, which eventually led to the **Latin** name **India**.
 
 
 
• **Tianzhu**:
 
 
• This was another historical **Chinese** name for **India**, especially used during the **Han Dynasty**.
 
• The term translates to "**Heavenly Center**," reflecting the high regard **Chinese** Buddhists had for **India** as the birthplace of **Lord Buddha**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Xuanzang's** travelogue, **"Great Tang Records on the Western Regions"**, is a primary source for the history of **India** during the reign of **King Harshavardhana**.
 
• Cultural and religious exchanges between **India** and **China** were primarily facilitated through the **Silk Road**, leading to the spread of **Buddhism** in **China**.
 
• The modern **Chinese** word for **India** is **Yindu**, which is a direct phonetic descendant of the ancient **Yintu**.
 
• The diverse names for **India** across different civilizations (**Hindustan**, **India**, **Yintu**) all share a common etymological root in the **Sindhu** (Indus) river.

questions.question: Loor' is a popular dance of which of the following Indian state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Haryana**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Loor** is a highly popular folk dance that belongs to the state of **Haryana**, India.
 
• The word **'Loor'** means **'girl'** in the local dialect of the **Bangar** region of **Haryana**, where the dance originated.
 
• It is traditionally performed exclusively by **women** and girls during the festive season of **Holi** and the arrival of the **spring** season.
 
• The dance is unique because it often involves a **thematic dialogue** in the form of questions and answers between two groups of dancers, usually centered around family life, marriage, or social customs.
 
• The **Loor** dance serves as a medium for young girls to express their joy and is often used to signal the beginning of the **Rabi crop** harvest. ***Hence, the correct answer is Haryana.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Other Folk Dances of Haryana:**

 
 
• **Dhamal Dance:** This is a traditional dance of **Haryana** that dates back to the era of the **Mahabharata**. It is primarily performed by men outdoors on moonlit nights during the month of **Phalguna**.
 
• **Phag Dance:** Performed by both men and women, this dance is specifically dedicated to celebrating the festival of **Holi** and the colorful atmosphere of the spring season.

• **Folk Dances of Goa:**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Loor** dance is most prominently seen in districts such as **Bhiwani**, **Dadri**, and **Jind** in **Haryana**.

• The **Shikaar Nritya**, also known as the **Hunting Dance**, is a traditional folk performance primarily associated with the **Siddi community** of **Gujarat**.

questions.question: ______ is present at the growing tips of stems and roots and increases the length of the stem and the root.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Apical meristem**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Apical meristem** is a type of **meristematic tissue** located at the **growing tips** of **stems** and **roots** of plants.
 
• The primary function of this tissue is to facilitate **primary growth**, which directly results in an **increase in the length** of the plant body.
 
• It consists of a group of **actively dividing cells** that are small, spherical, or polygonal in shape with **thin cellulose walls** and dense **cytoplasm**.
 
• In the **shoot system**, it is known as the **Shoot Apical Meristem (SAM)**, which gives rise to leaves and flowers, while in the **root system**, it is called the **Root Apical Meristem (RAM)**, responsible for penetrating deeper into the soil.
 
• As these cells divide, some remain in the meristem to maintain the growing point, while others **differentiate** into various **permanent tissues**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Lateral Meristem**:

 
 
• This tissue is found on the **lateral sides** of stems and roots.
 
• It is responsible for **secondary growth**, which increases the **girth** or **thickness** of the plant.
 
• Examples include the **vascular cambium** and **cork cambium** (phellogen), typically seen in woody **dicots** and **gymnosperms**.
 
 
 
• **Intercalary Meristem**:
 
 
• This meristem is located at the **base of leaves** or **internodes** (the regions between two nodes).
 
• It is particularly prominent in **monocots** like **grasses** and **bamboo**.
 
• It helps in the **regeneration** of parts removed by grazing herbivores and contributes to the **elongation** of the internodes.
 
 
 
• **Parenchyma Tissue**:
 
 
• Unlike meristematic tissues, **Parenchyma** is a type of **simple permanent tissue**.
 
• The cells are **living**, possess **thin cell walls**, and usually have large **vacuoles** for storage.
 
• Its functions include **photosynthesis** (when it contains chlorophyll, called **chlorenchyma**), **storage** of food/water, and providing **buoyancy** in aquatic plants (**aerenchyma**).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Meristematic Tissue Characteristics**: These cells have a **very high metabolic rate** and lack **vacuoles** because they are constantly dividing and do not need to store food or waste.
 
• **Differentiation**: This is the process where cells produced by the **meristem** take up a **permanent shape, size, and function** and lose the ability to divide further.
 
• **Plant Growth**: Unlike animals, plant growth is **localized** to specific regions containing meristematic tissues, which is why growth in plants is often considered **unlimited** or **indeterminate** at these specific points.
 
• **Classification**: Meristems are classified based on their **position** (Apical, Lateral, Intercalary) or their **origin** (Primary and Secondary meristems).

questions.question: In which part of the plant is the intercalary meristem typically located?

options.text: At the base of the flower

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Near the node**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Intercalary meristem** is a type of **primary meristematic tissue** that is located between regions of mature, permanent tissues. It is typically found **near the node**, at the base of the internodes, or at the **base of leaf blades** in plants.
 
• This tissue is responsible for the **longitudinal growth** of the plant, specifically contributing to the **elongation of internodes**. This allows stems to increase in length even if the apical meristem is distant.
 
• One of the most vital functions of the **intercalary meristem** is the **regeneration** of plant parts. In many **grasses**, this tissue allows the plant to regrow after the tips have been removed by grazing herbivores.
 
• These meristems are essentially remnants of the **apical meristem** that have been separated from the apex by the development of permanent tissues during the growth process.
 
• It is most commonly observed in **monocotyledonous plants** such as **bamboo**, **sugarcane**, and various types of **grasses**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Near the node.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Apical Meristem:**

 
 
• This tissue is located at the growing tips of **roots** and **shoots**.
 
• It is responsible for **primary growth**, which increases the height of the plant and the depth of the roots in the soil.
 
• The **root apical meristem** is found at the **root tip**, protected by the root cap, while the **shoot apical meristem** is found at the very tip of the stem.
 
 
 
• **Lateral Meristem:**
 
 
• These meristems are found on the lateral sides of **stems** and **roots**, running parallel to the long axis.
 
• They are responsible for **secondary growth**, which increases the **girth** or thickness of the plant.
 
• Common examples include the **vascular cambium** and **cork cambium** (phellogen), typically found in woody **dicotyledonous** plants and gymnosperms.
 
 
 
• **Meristematic Tissues:**
 
 
• These are groups of **undifferentiated cells** capable of active cell division throughout the life of the plant.
 
• Based on their **origin**, they are classified into **pro-meristem**, **primary meristem**, and **secondary meristem**.
 
• Cells in these tissues have **thin cellulose walls**, dense cytoplasm, and lack large vacuoles.
 
 
 
• **Permanent Tissues:**
 
 
• When meristematic cells lose their ability to divide, they take up a specific role and form **permanent tissues**.
 
• They are divided into **Simple Permanent Tissue** (like **Parenchyma**, **Collenchyma**, and **Sclerenchyma**) and **Complex Permanent Tissue** (like **Xylem** and **Phloem**).

questions.question: In which Indian state is 'Syalde Bikhauti Mela' celebrated?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Syalde Bikhauti Mela** is a prominent annual cultural fair celebrated in the **Kumaon** region of the Indian state of **Uttarakhand**.
 
• This fair takes place in the town of **Dwarahat**, located in the **Almora** district, and is held during the month of **April**, specifically coinciding with **Vishwat Sankranti** (the first day of the **Hindu** month of **Vaishakh**).
 
• The festival is divided into two distinct parts: **Syalde**, which is celebrated on the night before the main event, and **Bikhauti**, which is the primary celebration held on the day of the **Sankranti**.
 
• A unique and historical ritual of this fair is the **Oda-Bheta**, where devotees strike a particular stone with a stick to symbolize the victory over an ancient rival clan, the **Katpuria**, reflecting the region's martial history.
 
• The fair serves as a platform for the preservation of local folk traditions, featuring traditional dances like the **Jhora** and **Chanchari**, and folk songs that narrate the legends of the **Himalayan** foothills.
 
• Thousands of people from neighboring villages and tourists visit the **Shitaladevi Temple** during this period to seek blessings and participate in the vibrant festivities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cultural Landscape of Uttarakhand:** Known as **Devbhoomi** (Land of the Gods), **Uttarakhand** is home to two primary cultural zones, **Garhwal** and **Kumaon**, each hosting a variety of fairs linked to seasonal changes and religious legends.
 
• **Major Fairs in the State:**
 
 
• **Kumbh Mela:** Held in **Haridwar** every **12 years**, it is one of the largest religious congregations in the world and is recognized by **UNESCO** as an **Intangible Cultural Heritage**.
 
• **Nanda Devi Raj Jat:** A grand pilgrimage and fair that takes place once every **12 years**, tracing a long trek through the high-altitude mountains of **Chamoli**.
 
• **Bagwal Mela:** Celebrated at the **Devidhura** temple in **Champawat** district during **Raksha Bandhan**, it is famous for its ritualistic stone-pelting tradition.
 
• **Jauljibi Mela:** An international trade and cultural fair held at the confluence of the **Kali** and **Gori** rivers, facilitating exchange between people from **India**, **Nepal**, and **Tibet**.
 
 
 
• **Economic and Social Importance:** These melas (fairs) are not only religious events but also serve as important trade hubs for local artisans to sell traditional **Kumaoni** and **Garhwali** crafts, woolens, and organic mountain produce.
 
• **Festivals of Uttarakhand:** Other significant festivals include **Phool Dei** (the spring flower festival), **Harela** (marking the onset of the rainy season), and **Ghee Sankranti**, all of which emphasize the state's deep connection with nature and agriculture.

questions.question: Burrakatha', a traditional ballad that primarily narrates mythological stories, is a folk art of which Indian state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Andhra Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Burrakatha** is a highly popular and traditional **ballad** or folk narrative art form from the Indian state of **Andhra Pradesh** and **Telangana**.
 
• The name of the art form is derived from '**Burra**', which refers to the **tambura**, a stringed musical instrument shaped like a human skull (made of a hollowed-out gourd) used by the lead performer.
 
• A **Burrakatha** performance typically involves a troupe of three members: the lead storyteller called the **Kathakudu** and two side-performers who play the **Dakki** (a small drum).
 
• The primary objective of this art form was to narrate **mythological stories** from ancient Indian epics like the **Ramayana** and the **Mahabharata** to village audiences.
 
• During the **mid-20th century**, particularly during the **Indian Independence Movement**, Burrakatha evolved into a medium for **social and political awareness**, used to spread patriotic messages and educate the public on contemporary issues.
 
• In **1942**, the **Praja Natya Mandali** (People’s Theatre Association) popularized it further to reach the masses with messages of reform and revolution. ***Hence, the correct answer is Andhra Pradesh.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Roles of Performers:**

 
 
• The **Kathakudu** (Lead Singer) wears **Gajjalu** (anklets), plays the **Tambura**, and leads the narration with rhythmic movements.
 
• One assistant, known as the **Rajakiya**, provides political or social commentary, while the other, known as the **Hasyam**, provides comic relief to keep the audience engaged.
 
 
 
• **Cultural Significance:**
 
 
• It evolved from the **Jangam Katha** tradition of wandering minstrels who worshipped **Lord Shiva**.
 
• The language used is typically **Telugu**, and the performance involves a blend of **Sahitya** (literature), **Sangita** (music), and **Abhinaya** (expression).
 
 
 
• **Other Folk Arts of Andhra Pradesh:**
 
 
• **Kuchipudi**: The world-renowned classical dance form named after the village in **Krishna district**.
 
• **Butta Bommalu**: A folk dance where performers wear large **hollow masks/dolls** made of wood and dry grass.
 
• **Veeranatyam**: A religious dance associated with the worship of **Lord Veerabhadra**.
 
• **Lambadi**: A tribal dance associated with the **Banjara** community of the state.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other States:**
 
 
• **Kerala** is famous for **Kathakali** and **Mohiniyattam**.
 
• **Bihar** is known for **Jat-Jatin** and **Bideshiya** folk theatre.
 
• **Madhya Pradesh** is noted for the **Maach** folk drama and **Matki** dance.

questions.question: Why do people sprinkle water on roofs or open ground after a hot sunny day?

options.text: To increase the temperature of the surface.
To help water absorb the heat.
To utilize the large latent heat of vaporisation of water for cooling.
To make the surface more slippery.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To utilize the large latent heat of vaporisation of water for cooling**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When water is sprinkled on a hot roof or open ground, it undergoes the process of **evaporation**.
 
• **Evaporation** is a surface phenomenon where liquid molecules gain enough energy to transition into the **gaseous state** even below the boiling point.
 
• Water has a remarkably **large latent heat of vaporisation**, which is approximately **22.6 x 10⁵ J/kg** (or **540 calories per gram**).
 
• This **latent heat** refers to the "hidden" energy required to break the **intermolecular forces** (hydrogen bonds) between water molecules to convert them from liquid to steam without a change in temperature.
 
• To evaporate, the water droplets absorb this vast amount of **thermal energy** directly from the hot surface of the roof or the ground.
 
• As the surface loses its **heat energy** to the water, its **internal energy** decreases, leading to a significant drop in **temperature**. ***Hence, the statement in option 3 is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Latent Heat:** It is the **heat energy** absorbed or released by a substance during a change in its **physical state** (phase change) that occurs without changing its **temperature**. For water, the two main types are **latent heat of fusion** (melting) and **latent heat of vaporisation** (boiling/evaporating).
 
• **Specific Heat Capacity:** Water also has a very high **specific heat capacity** (about **4,184 J/kg·K**), meaning it can absorb a lot of heat before its own temperature rises significantly. This makes it an ideal **coolant** in various industrial and domestic applications.
 
• **Evaporative Cooling in Nature:**
 
 
• **Sweating:** Humans use the same principle to regulate body temperature. When **sweat** evaporates from the **skin**, it takes away **body heat**, providing a cooling sensation.
 
• **Earthen Pots (Matka):** In summer, water remains cool in **clay pots** because water seeps through **micro-pores** and evaporates from the outer surface, taking heat from the water inside.
 
 
 
• **Vaporisation vs. Boiling:** While **boiling** is a bulk phenomenon occurring at a specific **boiling point** (**100°C** for water at sea level), **evaporation** occurs at all temperatures and only at the **surface** of the liquid.
 
• **Factors Affecting Evaporation:** The rate of cooling through sprinkling water depends on the **surface area** (larger area increases evaporation), **humidity** (lower humidity increases evaporation), and **wind speed**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **latent heat of vaporisation** for water is much higher than that of most other common liquids, which is why it is the most effective substance for **cooling** hot surfaces during **summer**.
 
• While **conduction** and **convection** also play roles in heat transfer, the primary mechanism for the rapid cooling observed after sprinkling is **phase-change cooling** via evaporation.
 
• In **dry climates**, this method is extremely efficient, whereas in **high humidity**, the rate of evaporation slows down, making the cooling effect less pronounced.

questions.question: Which of the following language families is the most spoken in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indo-European**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Indo-European** language family, specifically the **Indo-Aryan** branch, is the most spoken language family in **India**, covering approximately **78.05%** of the total population as per the **2011 Census**.
 
• This family dominates the linguistic landscape of **Northern**, **Western**, **Central**, and **Eastern India**. It includes major languages such as **Hindi**, **Bengali**, **Marathi**, **Gujarati**, **Punjabi**, **Odia**, **Assamese**, **Urdu**, and **Sanskrit**. ***Hence, option 1 is correct.***
 
• **Hindi**, written in the **Devanagari** script, is the most widely spoken language within this family and serves as the **Official Language** of the **Union of India** under **Article 343** of the **Constitution**.
 
• The development of **Indo-Aryan** languages is generally divided into three stages: **Old Indo-Aryan** (represented by **Vedic Sanskrit**), **Middle Indo-Aryan** (including **Prakrit** and **Pali**), and **Modern Indo-Aryan** (the current vernaculars).
 
• The **Indo-Aryan** group is a branch of the **Indo-Iranian** subfamily, which in turn belongs to the **Indo-European** family, showing historical links between **Indian** languages and those spoken in **Europe** and **Iran**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dravidian Language Family:**

 
 
• This is the second-largest language family in **India**, spoken by about **19.64%** of the population.
 
• It is primarily concentrated in **Southern India** and includes the four major classical languages: **Telugu** (**6.70%**), **Tamil** (**5.70%**), **Kannada** (**3.61%**), and **Malayalam** (**2.88%**).
 
• Other minor languages in this family include **Tulu**, **Kodava**, **Gondi**, and **Kurukh**.
 
 
 
• **Austro-Asiatic Language Family:**
 
 
• Also known as the **Nishada** family, it is spoken by approximately **1.11%** of the **Indian** population.
 
• It is subdivided into the **Munda** group (spoken in **Central** and **Eastern India** like **Jharkhand** and **Odisha**) and the **Mon-Khmer** group (spoken in **Meghalaya** and the **Nicobar Islands**).
 
• Prominent languages include **Santali**, **Khasi**, **Ho**, and **Mundari**.
 
 
 
• **Tibeto-Burman Language Family:**
 
 
• Belonging to the broader **Sino-Tibetan** family, these languages are spoken by about **1.01%** of the population.
 
• They are prevalent in the **Himalayan** belt and **North-Eastern India**, including states like **Arunachal Pradesh**, **Manipur**, **Nagaland**, and **Mizoram**.
 
• Key languages include **Manipuri** (**Meitei**), **Bodo**, **Garo**, and **Lushai**.
 
 
 
• **Linguistic Diversity in India:**
 
 
• The **Eighth Schedule** of the **Indian Constitution** recognizes **22** major languages.
 
• The **Linguistic Survey of India**, initiated by **Sir George Abraham Grierson** in the late **19th century**, remains a foundational study of the country's diverse language groups.
 
• Apart from the four main families mentioned, **India** also has speakers of **Tai-Kadai** and **Great Andamanese** language groups.

questions.question:
What substances were used in the head of early matches to initiate combustion?

I. Antimony trisulphide

II. Potassium chlorate

III. White phosphorus
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**I, II and III**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The history of the modern match involves various chemical compositions. In the early **19th century**, the head of a friction match was made of a mixture of **Antimony trisulphide**, **Potassium chlorate**, and **White phosphorus** with some glue and starch.
 
• **Antimony trisulphide** (**Sb2S3**) served as the primary **combustible material** or fuel in the mixture. It provided the substance that would burn once the ignition temperature was reached. ***Hence, statement I is correct.***
 
• **Potassium chlorate** (**KClO3**) acted as a powerful **oxidizing agent**. In any combustion reaction, an oxidizer is required to provide **oxygen**; the potassium chlorate ensured that the reaction was rapid and vigorous once started. ***Hence, statement II is correct.***
 
• **White phosphorus** was the crucial component for **initiation**. It has a very low ignition temperature and would catch fire due to the heat generated by **friction** when the match was struck against a rough surface. ***Hence, statement III is correct.***
 
• This specific combination allowed the match to be "strike-anywhere," but the inclusion of white phosphorus proved to be extremely **hazardous** for both the users and the factory workers involved in the manufacturing process.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is I, II and III.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Evolution of Matches**: The first friction match was invented by **John Walker**, an English chemist, in **1826**. His initial version used **Antimony trisulphide** and **Potassium chlorate**, but it did not include phosphorus, making it difficult to ignite.
 
• **White Phosphorus Toxicity**: The use of **White phosphorus** led to a severe occupational disease called **"phossy jaw"** (phosphorus necrosis of the jaw). This condition caused the jawbone to decay and was often fatal for match-factory workers.
 
• **Transition to Safety Matches**: Due to the dangers of white phosphorus, **Safety Matches** were developed. In these, the **White phosphorus** was replaced by **Red phosphorus**, which is much less reactive and non-toxic.
 
• **Striking Surface**: In modern safety matches, the match head typically contains only **Potassium chlorate** and **Antimony trisulphide**, while the **Red phosphorus** is applied to the **striking surface** of the matchbox rather than the match head itself.
 
• **Chemical Reaction**: When a safety match is struck, the friction converts a small amount of **Red phosphorus** into **White phosphorus**, which then ignites and sets off the **Potassium chlorate** in the match head to burn the fuel.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Berne Convention (1906)**: This was an international agreement that effectively **banned** the use of **White phosphorus** in the manufacture of matches due to its extreme health risks.
 
• **Red vs. White Phosphorus**: While **White phosphorus** is **poisonous** and can spontaneously ignite in air, **Red phosphorus** is stable at room temperature and much safer to handle, which is why it is the standard in the industry today.
 
• **Ingredients for Friction**: Powdered **glass** is often added to the striking surface or the match head to increase **friction**, ensuring enough heat is generated to start the chemical reaction.

questions.question:
Which of the following is the main tool of monetary policy of the Reserve Bank of India?

 I . Reverse repo operations

 II . Transfer payments
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only I**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Reverse repo operations** are a fundamental **quantitative tool** of the **monetary policy** used by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** to control the **money supply** in the economy. Under this operation, the **RBI** borrows money from **commercial banks** by providing **government securities** as collateral, thereby absorbing **excess liquidity** from the banking system. ***Hence, statement I is correct.***
 
• **Transfer payments** are government expenditures for which no **goods or services** are received in return, such as **pensions**, **scholarships**, and **subsidies**. These are instruments of **Fiscal Policy**, which is managed by the **Government of India** (Ministry of Finance), rather than the **monetary policy** managed by the **central bank**. ***Hence, statement II is incorrect.***
 
• The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** is vested with the responsibility of conducting **monetary policy** under the provisions of the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**.
 
• The primary goal of the **RBI's monetary policy** is to maintain **price stability** (inflation targeting) while ensuring an adequate flow of **credit** to productive sectors to support **economic growth**.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Only I.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Repo Rate (Repurchase Rate)**:

 
 
• This is the **interest rate** at which the **RBI** lends money to **commercial banks** for **short-term** requirements against **government securities**.
 
• An **increase** in the **repo rate** makes borrowing expensive for banks, leading to a **decrease** in the **money supply** and helping to curb **inflation**.
 
 
 
• **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)**:
 
 
• It is the **percentage** of a bank's **total deposits** (Net Demand and Time Liabilities) that it must keep with the **RBI** in the form of **liquid cash**.
 
• The **RBI** does not pay any **interest** on the **CRR** balances maintained by banks.
 
 
 
• **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)**:
 
 
• Banks are required to maintain a certain **minimum percentage** of their **NDTL** in the form of **liquid assets** like **gold**, **cash**, or **unencumbered securities**.
 
• Unlike **CRR**, which is kept with the **RBI**, **SLR** is maintained by the **banks themselves**.
 
 
 
• **Qualitative Tools**:
 
 
• Besides **quantitative tools**, the **RBI** uses **qualitative** or **selective credit control** tools like **moral suasion**, **margin requirements**, and **rationing of credit** to regulate the **direction of credit** to specific sectors.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)**:

 
 
• The **MPC** was constituted under **Section 45ZB** of the **amended RBI Act, 1934** in **2016**.
 
• It consists of **six members**: three from the **RBI** (including the **Governor** as the **ex-officio Chairperson**) and three **external members** appointed by the **Central Government**.
 
• The **MPC** meets at least **four times a year** to decide the **Policy Repo Rate** to achieve the **inflation target**, which is currently set at **4%** with a tolerance band of **+/- 2%** (i.e., **2% to 6%**).
 
 
 
• **Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF)**:
 
 
• This facility allows **banks** to borrow money through **repurchase agreements (repos)** or to lend money to the **RBI** through **reverse repo agreements**.
 
• The **Reverse Repo Rate** is typically **lower** than the **Repo Rate**, creating a **corridor** for **short-term interest rates**.

questions.question: In 2019 , a new Rs. 20 coin was announced in the budget. The shape of this coin is ______ edged polygon.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**12**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The new **Rs. 20 coin** was first announced by the **Government of India** during the **Union Budget 2019**.
 
• The shape of the **Rs. 20 coin** is a **12-edged polygon**, technically known as a **dodecagon**. ***Hence, the correct answer is 12.***
 
• This coin was officially unveiled by **Prime Minister Narendra Modi** in **March 2019** as part of a new series of coins.
 
• The primary objective of the new design, including the **12-sided** shape, was to make the currency easily identifiable for **visually impaired** individuals.
 
• The coin has an **outside diameter** of **27 mm** and weighs approximately **8.54 grams**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Physical Composition**:

 
 
• The **Rs. 20 coin** is a **bi-metallic** coin, similar to the **Rs. 10 coin**.
 
• The **outer ring** is composed of **Nickel-Brass** (containing **75% Copper**, **20% Zinc**, and **5% Nickel**).
 
• The **inner center (piece)** is made of **Nickel-Brass** as well, but with a different golden-hued finish to distinguish the layers.
 
 
 
• **Design Features (Obverse)**:
 
 
• The face of the coin features the **Lion Capital of Ashoka Pillar** in the center.
 
• The words "**Satyamev Jayate**" are inscribed below the Lion Capital.
 
• The word "**Bharat**" in Hindi and "**INDIA**" in English are flank the left and right peripheries respectively.
 
 
 
• **Design Features (Reverse)**:
 
 
• The reverse side displays the denominational value "**20**" in the international numeral system.
 
• The **Rupee symbol (₹)** is placed above the numeral value.
 
• A motif of **grains** is depicted on the coin, symbolizing the **agricultural** foundation of the **Indian economy**.
 
• The **year of minting** is shown on the center-left of the reverse side.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **New Series of Coins**: Along with the **Rs. 20** denomination, the government released a new series of **Rs. 1, Rs. 2, Rs. 5, and Rs. 10** coins in **2019**.
 
• **Accessibility**: These coins were designed following the **National Institute of Design (NID)** guidelines to ensure they are **user-friendly** for the **divyangjan** (persons with disabilities).
 
• **Minting Locations**: These coins are produced at the **Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India Limited (SPMCIL)** mints located in **Mumbai**, **Kolkata**, **Hyderabad**, and **Noida**.
 
• **Coinage Act**: The issuance of these coins is governed by the **Coinage Act, 2011**, which gives the **Central Government** the power to design and mint coins of various denominations.

questions.question: The principal minerals produced in _______ are Gold Ore, Iron Ore, Limestone, Manganese Ore, Minor Mineral, and Vermiculite.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Andhra Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Andhra Pradesh** is one of the mineral-rich states in India, often referred to as the **Ratna Garbha** due to its vast and diverse mineral wealth. The state produces a wide array of minerals including **Gold Ore, Iron Ore, Limestone, Manganese Ore, Minor Minerals, and Vermiculite**.
 
• **Gold Ore**: In **Andhra Pradesh**, gold deposits are primarily found in the **Ramagiri Gold Fields** located in the **Ananthapuramu district**. Historically, these fields have been significant for gold prospecting in southern India. ***Hence, the statement regarding Gold Ore production is correct.***
 
• **Iron Ore**: The state possesses substantial reserves of iron ore, particularly **Hematite** and **Magnetite** types. These are located in districts such as **Anantapur, Kurnool, Kadapa, and Nellore**. These minerals serve as a crucial raw material for the local steel industries. ***Hence, the statement regarding Iron Ore is correct.***
 
• **Limestone**: **Andhra Pradesh** is a leading producer of **Limestone**, which is the backbone of the **Cement Industry**. Massive deposits are found in **Guntur, Kurnool, and Krishna** districts. The state contributes significantly to the national cement production capacity. ***Hence, the statement regarding Limestone is correct.***
 
• **Vermiculite and Manganese**: The state is the largest producer of **Vermiculite** in India, with major mines situated in the **Nellore** district. Additionally, **Manganese Ore** is predominantly found in the **Vizianagaram** and **Srikakulam** districts, contributing to the ferro-alloys sector. ***Hence, the statement regarding Manganese and Vermiculite is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mineral Diversity of Other States:**

 
 
• **Gujarat**: This state is a major producer of **Petroleum (Crude)**, **Natural Gas**, and **Lignite**. It also leads in the production of **Fluorite** and **Silica Sand**. The **Ankleshwar** and **Cambay** basins are famous for their hydrocarbon resources.
 
• **Assam**: Primarily known for its **Energy Minerals**. It is home to the oldest oil refinery in India at **Digboi**, established in **1901**. Major minerals include **Crude Oil, Natural Gas, and Coal** (Tertiary coal).
 
• **Rajasthan**: Known as the "Museum of Minerals," it has a monopoly over **Zinc, Lead, and Silver**. It also produces significant quantities of **Copper** (Khetri), **Gypsum**, and **Rock Phosphate**.
 
 
 
• **Barytes Production**: **Andhra Pradesh** holds the world's largest **Barytes** deposit at **Mangampet** in the **Kadapa** district. It accounts for more than **90%** of India's total Barytes production.
 
• **Regulatory Bodies**: Mineral exploration and data in India are managed by the **Geological Survey of India (GSI)** and the **Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM)**, established in **1851** and **1948** respectively.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Economic Impact**: The mining sector in **Andhra Pradesh** contributes roughly **3% to 4%** to the **State Gross Domestic Product (GSDP)**. The state government has implemented the **Andhra Pradesh Mineral Policy** to streamline licensing and promote sustainable mining.
 
• **Minor Minerals**: The state is famous for high-quality **Granite** (Galaxy Granite) and **Beach Sand Minerals** (Ilmenite, Rutile, Zircon) found along the coastline in **Visakhapatnam** and **Srikakulam**.
 
• **Classification**: Minerals in India are classified into **Major Minerals** (like Coal, Iron Ore, Gold) and **Minor Minerals** (like Sand, Gravel, Building Stones) as per the **Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957**.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a way by which an insect pests attack the plants?

options.text: They cut the root, stem and leaf
They suck the cell sap from various parts of the plant
They bore into stem and fruits

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They help in nitrogen fixation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Insect pests** are organisms that cause damage to **crops** and **plants**, leading to a reduction in **agricultural yield** and quality. They typically attack plants in three main ways: **cutting**, **sucking**, and **boring**.
 
• One common method is when pests **cut the root, stem, and leaf**. Insects such as **grasshoppers**, **caterpillars**, and **beetles** possess **biting and chewing mouthparts** (mandibles) that allow them to consume plant tissues. This destroys the photosynthetic area and structural integrity of the plant. ***Hence, statement 1 is a correct way of attack.***
 
• Another significant method of attack is when they **suck the cell sap from various parts of the plant**. Pests like **aphids**, **leafhoppers**, and **whiteflies** use **piercing and sucking mouthparts** (proboscis) to extract nutrient-rich fluids from the **phloem** or **xylem**. This leads to yellowing, curling of leaves, and overall wilting. ***Hence, statement 2 is a correct way of attack.***
 
• Certain pests also **bore into stems and fruits**. These are often referred to as **internal feeders**. Larvae of insects like the **stem borer** or **fruit borer** enter the internal tissues to feed, which often results in the death of the plant shoot or the destruction of the harvestable fruit. ***Hence, statement 3 is a correct way of attack.***
 
• **Nitrogen fixation** is a **biological process** by which **atmospheric nitrogen** is converted into **ammonia** or other molecules available to living organisms. This is primarily performed by **microorganisms** like **bacteria** (e.g., **Rhizobium**) and **blue-green algae**, often in a **symbiotic relationship** with plant roots. Insect pests do not perform this function; instead, their presence usually hinders the plant's ability to thrive. ***Hence, statement 4 is NOT a way of attack and is the correct answer.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Classification of Insect Pests:**

 
 
• **Chewing Insects:** These include **locusts**, **termites**, and **larvae of lepidoptera**. They physically remove plant parts, reducing the **leaf area index**.
 
• **Sucking Insects:** These include **thrips** and **bugs**. Besides draining nutrients, they often act as **vectors** for **plant viruses**, causing secondary infections.
 
• **Boring Insects:** These include **weevils** and **borers**. They are difficult to control because they live inside the plant protected from many surface-applied **pesticides**.
 
 
 
• **Economic Impact:**
 
 
• Insect pests can cause **crop losses** ranging from **10% to 30%** annually, depending on the **geographical location** and the **pest density**.
 
• The **Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)** estimates that pests destroy up to **40% of global food crops** each year.
 
 
 
• **Biological Nitrogen Fixation (BNF):**
 
 
• This process occurs in the **root nodules** of **leguminous plants** (like **pulses**, **beans**, and **peas**).
 
• The enzyme **nitrogenase** catalyzes the conversion of **Nitrogen gas (N2)** into **Ammonia (NH3)**.
 
• This is a vital part of the **Nitrogen Cycle**, enriching the **soil fertility** naturally without the need for **chemical fertilizers**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Integrated Pest Management (IPM):** This is a **sustainable approach** to managing pests by combining **biological**, **cultural**, and **chemical tools** in a way that minimizes economic, health, and environmental risks.
 
• **Natural Enemies:** Not all insects are pests. **Predatory insects** like **ladybird beetles** and **parasitoid wasps** help control pest populations, acting as **biological control agents**.
 
• **Host Plant Resistance:** Some plants have evolved **morphological features** (like **thick cuticles** or **hairs**) or **biochemical defenses** (**toxins**) to resist attack from cutting, sucking, or boring insects.

questions.question: Daskathia is a form of ballad singing prevalent in ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Odisha**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Daskathia** is a traditional and highly popular form of **folk ballad singing** that is indigenous to the state of **Odisha**, particularly prevalent in the **Ganjam** district.
 
• The performance gets its name from **Kathia**, which are **wooden clappers** (usually made of **teak** or **gambhari** wood) held in the hands to produce a rhythmic beat. The word **Das** translates to a devotee.
 
• This art form is traditionally performed by **two male artists**: the **Gayaka**, who is the lead singer and narrator, and the **Palia**, who acts as the assistant or co-singer.
 
• The primary themes of Daskathia revolve around **mythological stories**, specifically the legends of **Lord Shiva** (also known as **Rudra**). Because of its focus on **Shiva**, it is frequently referred to as **Rudra Natak**.
 
• During the performance, the **Gayaka** narrates the story through songs and prose, while the **Palia** provides the rhythmic accompaniment and repeats the refrains, often adding **humor** and **satire** to engage the audience. ***Hence, the correct answer is Odisha__.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Odisha's Other Folk Arts**:

 
 
• **Pala**: Another major narrative folk form in **Odisha** that combines elements of **Sanskrit drama** and local **Odia** poetry. Unlike Daskathia, it involves a larger group of **five to six performers** and uses instruments like the **Mridanga** and **Cymbals**.
 
• **Ghumura**: A traditional **folk dance** from the **Kalahandi** district of **Odisha**, known for its distinct **drum** (Ghumura) and energetic movements.
 
 
 
• **Punjab**:
 
 
• The state is famous for vibrant dance forms like **Bhangra** and **Gidda**. In terms of balladry, **Jugni** and **Heer-Ranjha** are significant musical and oral traditions.
 
 
 
• **Maharashtra**:
 
 
• **Powada** is the traditional ballad form of **Maharashtra**, used to narrate the heroic deeds of **Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj** and other historical figures. **Lavani** is the state's most famous folk dance.
 
 
 
• **Tamil Nadu**:
 
 
• The state features **Villu Paatu** (Bow Song), a narrative form where a **musical bow** is used as the primary instrument to tell tales of heroes and gods.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Performance Attire**: The performers usually wear **colorful dhotis** and **turbans**. The **Gayaka** often wears a **silk scarf** (Uttariya) and **bead necklaces**, maintaining a regal and devotional appearance.
 
• **Cultural Significance**: While it originated as a purely **religious** performance dedicated to **Lord Shiva**, modern Daskathia also incorporates stories from the **Ramayana** and the **Mahabharata** to cater to a broader audience.
 
• **The Instrument**: The **Kathia** clappers are about **six inches** long and are held between the fingers of the **left hand**, while the **right hand** is used to strike them, creating a sharp, rhythmic sound that keeps the pace of the narration.
 
• **Language**: The medium of performance is predominantly **Odia**, specifically the regional dialect of **South Odisha**, which adds a distinct flavor to the **ballad singing**.
